title: Black Wall Street, Ep. 1 — The Elevator
evidence_boundary: Survivor-memory retelling of the documented 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre. Narrator and family are fictional; surrounding events follow the record. Visuals are James's hand-curated selects.
desired_movement: Campfire testimony over James's curated noir imagery.
grounding: Her porch, the fire, the brass elevator box, the tracks.
invitation: Ten parts, one story, told to you by the fire.

scenes.text: [soft laugh] Come close, baby... this fire don't reach far. They want me to talk into that little machine there. [sighs] A hundred and six years old. ... Alright then. Let me reach back... and get it for you. All of it.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, front porch at night, rocking chair, oil lantern glow, quilt over the rail

scenes.text: Greenwood. [proud] North side of Tulsa. White folks called it Black Wall Street. We just called it OURS. [warm] Every face on that street knew your mama. That's the part... [quiet] no book ever got right.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, prosperous Black business district street, brick storefronts, striped awnings, people in Sunday hats

scenes.text: [bright] We had a hotel so fine the floors talked back when you walked! A picture theater... seats clean to the back of forever. [soft laugh] And a piano somewhere going ALL night long. [wistful] Lord... that piano.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, ornate theater marquee lit at dusk on a brick main street

scenes.text: [thoughtful] A dollar didn't leave our neighborhood in a hurry. Barber... to the grocer... to the church plate. Taking its sweet time. [warm] Daddy said that's what respect looks like... when it circulates.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, shopkeeper hands passing a dollar bill across a worn wooden counter, general store shelves

scenes.text: My daddy doctored folks up a narrow stair, name in gold paint on the glass. [inhales] Iodine and peppermint, that's what it smelled like up there. [soft laugh] Mama nursed beside him... when she wasn't nursing me.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, frosted glass office door with gold leaf physician lettering, narrow wooden staircase, oil sconce

scenes.text: [laughs] I was EIGHT. One good ribbon, and patent shoes that pinched like a crawdad! In the one photograph we saved, somebody tinted my ribbon pink by hand. [tender] I loved that ribbon more than some people.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, family of three on a wooden porch in Sunday best, small girl with pink hair ribbon, formal portrait

scenes.text: [thoughtful] Daddy used to say Greenwood got built twice. Once inside somebody's head... once in brick. Took me eighty years to understand him. [gentle] Everything you ever seen... started as a dream somebody KEPT.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, rows of new brick buildings with scaffolds, morning light, builders at work in the distance

scenes.text: Monday. Memorial Day. [uncertain] Must have been the last of May... flags was out, stores was shut. [low] Now hold my hand through this next part, baby. [whispers] This is where it turns.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, American flags on quiet storefronts, closed shop signs, empty morning street

scenes.text: [fond] There was a boy shined shoes downtown. Everybody called him Diamond Dick. [soft laugh] PRETTY boy. Grin like he owed you money and knew you'd forgive him. [pause] His given name? Gone, child. The grin stayed.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, young Black man at a shoeshine stand, warm grin, customer shoe on the brass rest

scenes.text: [flat] A colored man couldn't use just any washroom downtown. The one they left us sat at the TOP of a tall building. You rode a little elevator to get there. [tired] That's all that boy went to do. Ride up. Come down.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, tall downtown office building, stone facade and revolving door, pedestrians in boaters

scenes.text: A girl ran that elevator. Young. White. [dry] I never learned her name long enough to forget it. [slow] Two children... in a brass box... and history squeezing in there with them. It's a small room, history. Fits anywhere.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, ornate brass scissor-gate elevator interior, operator stool, overhead lamp, empty

scenes.text: [quick] The car jumped. He stumbled. His hand caught her arm, the way you'd catch ANYBODY. [sharp] And she hollered. And he RAN. [heavy] Because a colored boy in that town knew arithmetic... and a holler was a number too big.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, elevator floor indicator dial above closed doors, dramatic shadow

scenes.text: [bitter] A clerk next door heard the scream... and let his imagination finish the story. That's ALL it took, sugar. One man's imagination. [whispers] Fear writes fast. And it don't stop to check its spelling.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, clothing store window with suited mannequins, a running silhouette reflected in the glass

scenes.text: Now here's what they don't tell you. [conspiratorial] The police wasn't even SURE anything happened. The girl wouldn't swear to nothing. On any honest day... that's where it dies. [cold] It just wasn't going to be an honest day.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, police station front desk, open ledger book, officer cap resting on the counter

scenes.text: [soft] That night we slept easy, under our own roofs. [sighs] You don't know a sleep is precious... till you count how few you got left. [long pause] That was the last easy one... for a long, long while.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, dusk over district rooftops, chimneys and a church steeple, warm amber sky

scenes.text: Tuesday morning they came got Diamond Dick anyway. Quiet. Set him in the courthouse jail. [thoughtful] The sheriff... Mac-something. Big square man. Held them keys HONEST. [warm] Remember him kind, whoever he was.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, courthouse jail corridor, iron bars, single wooden chair, one shaft of window light

scenes.text: [tender] Greenwood didn't know one thing yet. Supper going... piano tuning up... men sweeping their own doorsteps. [firm] We was rich the way that COUNTS, baby. We belonged to each other. You hear me? Belonged.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, evening street with lit shop windows, cafe chairs, a broom leaning on a doorframe

scenes.text: [serious] But downtown... there was an afternoon paper needed selling. [angry] And there is no cheaper kindling on God's green earth than a white girl's scream and a Black boy's name set in the same line of type.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, newspaper building at dusk, tall lit windows, newsprint rolls stacked at the dock

scenes.text: I can't quote you the headline. I was eight years old. [low] But grown folks said it plain: that paper all but printed an INVITATION. [whispers] Come to the courthouse tonight. ... Bring your rope.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, linotype machine closeup, rows of metal type, operator hands at the keys

scenes.text: [cold] And here is the part that makes my hands cold. Go LOOK for that page today. Torn out. Every copy. Every archive. One careful hand. [slow] Paper can be cut, baby. ... What I carry can't.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, newspaper with a ragged torn-out column on dark wood beside a lamp

scenes.text: [urgent] Papers hit the street middle of the afternoon. Newsboys hollering it corner to corner. Folks said you could stand on our side of the tracks... and FEEL it coming. [hushed] Like weather. Like a green sky.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, newsboys with paper bundles on a corner, men in hats reaching for copies

scenes.text: [grim] By suppertime, the talk downtown was rope. They'd lynched a white boy in that same town not a YEAR before... and the law just watched. [bitter] Everybody knew the recipe worked. [pause] Everybody.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, empty town square at dusk, long shadows, courthouse in the distance

scenes.text: Come dark, they was collecting at the courthouse. Hundreds first. [rising] Then more than I got numbers for. [relieved] And that sheriff, bless him, barred his own doors and told that crowd ONE word. [firm] No.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, courthouse at night, dense crowd of men in hats outside, lit windows

scenes.text: [proud] And down our way... men who had SOLDIERED in France set down their suppers, and stood up. Some still had the Army coat. If the law couldn't hold the line, they would. [measured] That's not rage, child. That's arithmetic.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, formal studio portrait of Black World War One soldiers in uniform, campaign hats, dignified

scenes.text: [tense] Daddy locked the office early. Mama held my hand too tight the whole walk home... I taste copper just TELLING it. [whispers] The air had changed. You could feel tomorrow coming. And it was coming armed.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, night street, two figures walking under gas lamps, long shadows

scenes.text: [whispers] One gun is going to go off outside that courthouse, baby. Nobody will ever know whose finger. [pause] And the whole world... is going to tear its shirt. [gentle] But that's tomorrow's telling. Not tonight's.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, single revolver lying on stone courthouse steps in lamplight

scenes.text: [warm] This here is part one of ten. I'm telling it ALL, start to finish, right on this channel. [soft laugh] Go find part two when you're ready. The fire will still be lit... [tender] and I will still be here.
scenes.query: 1920s mood, porch at night, empty rocking chair, lantern burning low

voice_direction: 106-year-old survivor by the fire: laughs, whispers, slows down, speeds up, gets upset, gets tender. Inline v3 tags are intentional.
